title: START Triage Protocol (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment)

protocol.assessment: The START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) protocol is used in mass casualty incidents (MCI) to rapidly classify patients into four categories based on three physiological criteria: Respiration (R), Perfusion (P), and Mental status (M). The goal is to identify patients who need immediate life-saving intervention and allocate limited resources efficiently. Each patient assessment should take no more than 30-60 seconds.
steps: 1. STEP 1 - WALKING FILTER: Direct all ambulatory victims to move to a designated area. All patients who can walk are tagged GREEN (minor/delayed). This clears the scene and reduces the patient count for individual assessment.

2. STEP 2 - ASSESS RESPIRATION (R): Approach each remaining (non-ambulatory) patient. Check if the patient is breathing. If NOT breathing, reposition the airway (head-tilt chin-lift or jaw thrust). If breathing starts after repositioning, tag RED (immediate). If still not breathing after airway repositioning, tag BLACK (deceased/expectant).

3. STEP 3 - RESPIRATORY RATE: If the patient IS breathing, count the respiratory rate. If the respiratory rate is GREATER THAN 30 breaths per minute, tag RED (immediate). Tachypnea above 30/min indicates shock, respiratory distress, or metabolic crisis requiring immediate intervention.

4. STEP 4 - ASSESS PERFUSION (P): If the respiratory rate is 30 or fewer, assess perfusion. Check for a radial pulse. If the radial pulse is ABSENT, tag RED (immediate). Absent radial pulse indicates systolic blood pressure below approximately 80 mmHg (significant hemorrhage or shock). Alternatively, perform the capillary refill test: press the nail bed for 2 seconds; if refill takes MORE THAN 2 seconds, tag RED.

5. STEP 5 - CONTROL HEMORRHAGE: For any RED-tagged patient with life-threatening hemorrhage, apply a tourniquet or direct pressure before moving to the next patient. This is the ONLY treatment intervention performed during START triage.

6. STEP 6 - ASSESS MENTAL STATUS (M): If perfusion is adequate (radial pulse present or capillary refill under 2 seconds), assess mental status. Give a simple command: 'Squeeze my hand' or 'Open your eyes.' If the patient CANNOT follow simple commands, tag RED (immediate).

7. STEP 7 - TAG YELLOW: If the patient is breathing (rate 30 or under), has adequate perfusion (radial pulse present), AND can follow simple commands, tag YELLOW (delayed). These patients have serious injuries but are physiologically stable enough to wait for treatment.

8. STEP 8 - REASSESS: After all patients have been triaged, begin reassessment. Triage categories can change rapidly. RED patients who deteriorate may become BLACK. YELLOW patients may deteriorate to RED. Reassess every 5-10 minutes or whenever resources become available.
do_not: Do NOT spend more than 60 seconds on any single patient during initial START triage. The purpose is rapid sorting, not treatment. Move on to the next patient after tagging.

Do NOT perform CPR during START triage in a mass casualty incident. Patients who are not breathing after airway repositioning are tagged BLACK. CPR consumes resources that can save multiple other patients.
Do NOT transport GREEN-tagged patients before RED and YELLOW patients. GREEN patients are ambulatory and can wait. Use available transport for RED patients first, then YELLOW.
Do NOT skip the walking filter. It is the fastest way to reduce the number of patients requiring individual assessment and prevents overwhelm.
protocol.when_to_escalate: Escalate immediately when: (1) the number of RED-tagged patients exceeds available ALS transport capacity, (2) the MCI involves chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear (CBRN) agents requiring specialized decontamination, (3) pediatric patients are involved (use JumpSTART instead of START for children under 8), (4) the incident is expanding (active threat, secondary devices, structural collapse progression), or (5) triage resources are insufficient to complete initial assessment within 15 minutes.
